slides.text: Assalamu alaikum. We are team DecisionGuard, from the Bangladesh University of Professionals. DecisionGuard is a finance copilot for small Bangladeshi shops. It covers the three areas of Topic E: financing that fits, cash-flow alerts, and business analysis. One rule shapes everything you will see. Code computes every number, the language model only explains it, and nothing that matters happens until the owner approves it.

The problem is the same in Dhaka and in Shenzhen. Small firms are short of credit. The IFC puts the gap at 5.7 trillion dollars across developing economies, and about 2.8 billion dollars in Bangladesh, where women-led firms get only 7.28 percent of small-business credit. And cash gets stuck: in a Peking University survey of over nine thousand Chinese small firms, 71 percent were owed money they had not been paid. Lenders say no because these shops cannot show a clean record, not because the businesses are bad.

Picture the owner of a grocery in Mirpur. Her money moves through bKash and Nagad, a bank account and a cash box, and her credit sales live in a paper baki register. She has three questions, and they are exactly the three areas of Topic E. Which loan is really the cheapest, and can I get it? Will I run short of cash, when, and what can I do about it today? And is my business actually doing well? Everything in this demo runs on five synthetic Dhaka shops with eighteen months of daily records, clearly labelled as synthetic.

Why not just put a chatbot on top of the ledger? Because language models are not calculators. They pick the wrong figure, rarely catch their own mistakes, and sound more confident than they are. With money, a guessed number becomes a wrong decision. So DecisionGuard splits the work. Code computes every number with exact decimal arithmetic, and records where each number came from. The model only plans and explains. And any number the model states is recomputed before the owner sees it.

Here is the whole pipeline. The shop's own records come in: mobile-money and bank statements, the cash book, the baki register, even a photo of a receipt. They become typed facts. Bangla and Banglish are read correctly, names and phone numbers become tokens, and every row remembers where it came from. Deterministic engines compute everything from those facts. The copilot plans and explains. Anything that leaves DecisionGuard needs the owner's approval with a one-time code. And any number on any screen can be tapped to show its formula and the rows behind it.

Area B, cash flow. DecisionGuard forecasts thirteen weeks ahead with a thousand simulated paths, built from the shop's own weekday, month-end and Eid patterns, and from how late each customer usually pays. For our synthetic hardware shop, there is an 86.7 percent chance of a cash gap that starts in five days, with an expected shortfall of about 73 thousand taka. Every possible fix is measured on the same thousand paths, so the difference is the fix, not luck. The cheapest one, asking a buyer to pay early, closes almost the whole gap at no cost, and it arrives as an action card for the owner to approve.

Area A, financing. Lenders quote headline rates, so DecisionGuard turns every option into dated cash flows and solves for the true yearly cost, fees included. The same 9 percent headline costs 11.29 percent a year as a normal bank loan, and 22.15 percent as a digital loan repaid in daily debits. Our catalogue holds 13 real Bangladeshi loan products, each with its source and the date we checked it. If a lender asks for a fact we do not hold, DecisionGuard says not on record. It never assumes a pass.

Area C, analysis. DecisionGuard builds cash-basis statements and thirteen ratios, each one clickable down to the transactions, and it compares decisions before the owner makes them. Here, five options for the same hardware shop are replayed on the same thousand paths across forty economic states. A loan barely helps, because it pays out after the gap starts. Offering one large customer two percent off for paying early costs 7,600 taka, and cuts the risk of dipping below the buffer from 94 to 52 percent. The advice held in 8 of 10 stress re-runs, and never changed when we only shuffled rows or renamed customers.

The copilot is where most AI products cut corners, so we built five steps around the model. First, every question is screened for prompt injection in four languages. Second, a model proposes a plan, and code removes anything it does not recognise. The owner's own question decides what is answered first, so asking about a loan gets the loan, not every report. Third, every number in the answer is recomputed by an independent path. Fourth, a model from a different family argues the case against. Fifth, if checks fail or votes disagree, DecisionGuard says I don't know, and names what is missing.

Here is something no single-shop tool can do. These three synthetic shops owe each other in a circle: 11.5 lakh taka of debt, with each shop waiting for the next to pay. Minimum-cost netting clears all of it with 1.9 lakh taka of cash, moving only along debts that already exist. Every owner must approve with a one-time code, and one refusal cancels the round. The settled record is sealed with a salted hash that can be anchored on the Ethereum Sepolia testnet, so anyone can later check it was not edited, without the chain ever seeing a name or an amount.

Security comes down to one promise: money never moves without the owner. Every action has a tier. Anything that leaves DecisionGuard is execute tier: the owner approves that exact card with a fresh one-time code, and the policy is checked again when it runs. Four actions are denied to everyone, including the owner. The audit log is a hash chain the database refuses to edit, and only anonymised text can reach a model. Our injection guard is rules only. On a fresh held-out set it caught 15 of 24 attacks and wrongly blocked 10 of 24 innocent questions. So we do not rely on it: an injected instruction still needs the owner's one-time code before anything happens.

Everything we show is backed by evidence you can rerun. More than 2,500 automated tests, and none of them calls a model or the network. A sandbox log of 48 steps through the real API, from sign-in to an approved and audited action. Thirteen real loan products, each with its source. And the app speaks English, Bangla and Chinese. Every pull request runs lint, tests, dependency audits and a secret scan, then boots the whole stack. The evidence index in the repository lists every file and the command that regenerates it.

We want to be clear about what is not proven yet. All demo data is synthetic, and no real shop has used DecisionGuard. The injection guard is rules only, so the approval rules, not the guard, keep money safe. The copilot was measured offline, not with live models at scale. Receivables and message drafts are reduced, with no sending. Market prices are public lists from Bangladesh and China, as published, not live, and vendor quotes are synthetic. Next, we want to pilot with consenting Dhaka shops using their own bKash and Nagad exports, send approved reminders through SMS partners, bring in licensed lenders to fund netting rounds, and add a learned injection classifier with an external security review.

DecisionGuard gives a small shop owner numbers she can check, and actions she approves. Code computes every figure, the copilot explains it and checks itself, and nothing that matters happens without her one-time code. Thank you. Dhonnobad. Shieh shieh. The code, the documentation and the evidence are all in our repository.
